accuracy.evidence: Standards checked against the CCSS ELA Speaking and Listening text: SL.K.4 to SL.3.4 (describe people, places, things and events with relevant, descriptive details), SL.K.6 (speak audibly, express thoughts, feelings and ideas clearly) and SL.2.4 (speaking audibly in coherent sentences); and the English national curriculum spoken language statements (speak audibly and fluently; well-structured descriptions and narratives) plus Year 2 grammar (expanded noun phrases for description). Every toy and person round has exactly one item matching all its details, verified by tracing the crossing-out logic.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips teachers report in early speaking: vague words (nice, fun, kind, lovely) that cross nothing out, details that are true of everything or wrong for the object, events told out of order or ending first, and mixing up loud with clear so the child shouts or races. Each is a lab outcome, a prediction or a tagged challenge option.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdesc is a listener-guessing game: each spoken detail filters six drawn toys or people and visibly crosses out non-matches, a five-step voice dial is judged against three rows of listeners, event cards fill First/Next/Then/Last slots, and beach phrases are sorted by sense. No other flag lab filters candidates by spoken attributes; the 6-token shingle gate passed against every flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers that 'nice' leaves all six toys standing while 'small' halves them, that a whisper reaches only the front row and a shout makes every listener say ouch, and that a mixed-up order is refused until the start comes first. The step text only names what the screen already showed.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'It is nice' lets Kit find the toy (nothing gets crossed out); shouting is the best fix for the back row (the shout level triggers ouch on every face); and order does not matter (cards placed out of order are rejected with the reason).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers: 'vague' and 'bare' explain why nice or just 'a dog' cannot be pictured, 'shout' and 'fast' separate loud and quick from clear, 'mid' and 'end' fix sequencing, 'seebell' and 'touch' say ring is a sound, and 'nofeel' and 'nowhy' ask for a feeling word plus because.

readability.evidence: Family audience: kid text FK grade -1.0 and adult text FK 6.0 (limits 6.5 and 9.5), from learn/readability.py. Kid lines are short and concrete (a small red ball with spots); adult text uses the exact curriculum terms: relevant details, speak audibly, adjectives, expanded noun phrases, sense words and time connectives.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matched and explanation overlap with every other lesson is under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph is one idea with a worked example; adult paragraphs give the standards, the description toolkit, named mistakes with what to ask instead, and what each lab step does.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 Android in dark and light for all six steps: six picture cards in a 3x2 grid, word buttons wrap in rows below the canvas, the voice dial spans the width, and the four order slots stack full width. Red and blue toys first looked pink in dark mode, so fixed hues were set and rechecked. walk.cjs passes on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe reports no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark; every canvas action has a button (each detail word, quieter/louder/Speak now, Put the next card, See/Hear/Smell/Touch) and the canvas aria-label is updated with every spoken result. Show me finishes all five tasks within the 6 second limit.

sources: Common Core State Standards for ELA: Speaking and Listening SL.K.4, SL.K.6, SL.1.4, SL.2.4, SL.3.4
DfE (2013) English programmes of study KS1 and KS2: spoken language statements; Year 2 grammar (expanded noun phrases)
Voice 21 / Oracy Framework (physical: voice projection and pace; linguistic: vocabulary, structure)
